content.english: Yah, my song, has commanded you,
the people of Israel, with [a day of] your rest:
Keep the Sabbath day.
It shall be a sign between me and you.
Yah, my song, has commanded you,
the people of Israel, with [a day of] your rest:
Keep the Sabbath day.
It shall be a sign between me and you.
It is the holiest of days,
the hidden light, the secret for the upright,
the great allusion, the scent of incense,
a law for all time for all your generations.
Yah, my song, has commanded you,
the people of Israel, with [a day of] your rest:
Keep the Sabbath day.
It shall be a sign between me and you.
Look and learn how holy the Sabbath is:
like the Day of Atonement of the seventh month,
and even like the seventh year of freedom!
This is your wisdom and discernment.
Yah, my song, has commanded you,
the people of Israel, with [a day of] your rest:
Keep the Sabbath day.
It shall be a sign between me and you.
The Awesome One prepared the fats of the earth: / two days’ worth of food today!
Eat, my people! Today is the Sabbath, / forever kept holy for you!
Yah, my song, has commanded you,
the people of Israel, with [a day of] your rest:
Keep the Sabbath day.
It shall be a sign between me and you.
The bread is from heaven.
He sent provisions for the living:
It would not rot for two days,
so that your future generations would know!
Yah, my song, has commanded you,
the people of Israel, with [a day of] your rest:
Keep the Sabbath day.
It shall be a sign between me and you.

introduction:
Introduction

יה זמרתי, Yah Zimrati

Introduction: A poem for the Sabbath day, praising God and the holiness of the Sabbath. The poet compares the Sabbath to other Jewish traditions linked with the number seven: Yom Kippur in the seventh month of the year, the sabbatical year in the Land of Israel, and the seven days spent in booths on the Festival of Sukkot. The Sabbath must be celebrated with food of high quality, as learned from the experiences of the Israelites in the wilderness, where God supplied them with two days’ worth of food. While we presently do not have firm insight as to who wrote the poem, Yah Zimrati is included in the Venice Karaite siddur; thus, the author must have lived prior to 1528.

Category: Zemirot (Songs)

Genre: Zemer for the Sabbath

Occasion: Sabbath

Name: יה זמרתי, Yah Zimrati

Composer: Yehuda (otherwise unknown)

Acrostic: יהודה, “Yehuda”

Date: Before 1528

Meter: Eight syllables per line, with each sheva counting as a full syllable.

Source: Vilna Siddur, Volume 4, page 105. (However, in the fourth stanza, the first word of the second line is printed here as לחם, in accordance with the reading found in the Venice Siddur.)

Davidson number: י 4369

Karaite origin: Yes
